{"id": "20:132/q09", "question": "How did ʿUrwa apply these verses when he saw worldly goods?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q09/p1", "position": "He went home, recited the warning against coveting rulers' or wealthy people's goods, and called his household to prayer.", "reasons": "Hishām's reports and later accounts vary between seeing rulers' possessions, news of rulers, or anything worldly; Qurṭubī adds that he prayed, and Durr also reports his advice that anyone dazzled by worldly adornment should do this."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q10", "question": "How did ʿUmar apply this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q10/p1", "position": "He prayed at night, woke his household near its end for prayer, and recited the verse.", "reasons": "Aslam's account appears in Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, Durr, and al-Ālūsī; details vary between night and near dawn."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q11", "question": "What other household practice is reported?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q11/p1", "position": "Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Muzanī told his family to rise and pray in hardship.", "reasons": "Nasafī says he cited God's command. Ibn al-Jawzī-zād reports Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Muzanī saying this in household hardship, calling prayer God's and His Messenger's command, and reciting the verse."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q12", "question": "What does iṣṭabir ʿalayhā ask of the Prophet?", "turns_on": "Whether the stress is ordinary persistence, the intensified form's effort, or plentiful voluntary observance.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q12/p1", "position": "Persist patiently in performing prayer, enjoining it, and observing its demands.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Ṭabarī, Māwardī, Jishumī, Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ṭabrisī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn Kathīr, al-Ālūsī, and Islahi describe continued performance. Ṭabarī specifies prayer's limits; Rāzī says the Prophet should embody what he enjoins; Islahi likens persistence to a farmer tending a field until it yields."}, {"id": "20:132/q12/p2", "position": "It calls for strenuous effort beyond simple patience.", "reasons": "Burhān says the augmented form is stronger than aṣbir; Biqāʿī says iftiʿāl signals effort even when prayer consumes livelihood time; al-Ālūsī infers that fully observing worship is difficult for the soul. Al-Sāmarrāʾī explains the intensified form by prayer's daily recurrence and the substantial patience needed to complete it properly at appointed times."}, {"id": "20:132/q12/p3", "position": "It is abundant voluntary prayer, with the Prophet asked to persist even more than his family.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr takes iṣṭibār as restraint and its figurative sense as plentiful voluntary prayer, citing 73:1–2 and 17:79."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q13", "question": "How do inward readers distinguish iṣṭibār from ordinary patience?", "turns_on": "The inward accounts differ on whether the added quality is stillness, struggle, or being comforted beyond pain.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q13/p1", "position": "It is inner stillness under trial, in the heart and secret as well as the lower self.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ calls this the greatest or hardest patience, contrasting it with ordinary patience of the self; Sulamī and Bursevī transmit the formulation."}, {"id": "20:132/q13/p2", "position": "It is a station of struggle, whereas patience is a station of witnessing.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports the distinction from ʿArāʾis al-Baqlī."}, {"id": "20:132/q13/p3", "position": "It surpasses patience because divine support carries the person without felt pain.", "reasons": "Qushayrī describes the extra quality of istiṣbār in these terms."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q14", "question": "What inward meaning is given to the family's prayer?", "turns_on": "Whether inward prayer is a maintained bond, graded forms of presence, or discipline of inner faculties.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q14/p1", "position": "It means joining God and steadfastly maintaining that connection.", "reasons": "Sulamī reports Junayd, who says only the divinely supported can bear this connection."}, {"id": "20:132/q14/p2", "position": "It means presence of heart and a graded prayer of body, soul, heart, secret, and spirit.", "reasons": "Sulamī reports learning prayer as presence. Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh likens prayer and fasting to the warp and weft of worshippers' robes. Bursevī expands this into bodily obligatory and voluntary prayer, the soul's ascent, the heart's vigilance, the secret's exclusive witnessing, and the spirit's annihilation and abiding through God, citing 89:29–30, 23:2, and 4:80."}, {"id": "20:132/q14/p3", "position": "It directs inner faculties toward presence, obedience, struggle, and unveiling.", "reasons": "Qāshānī treats ahl as psychic and spiritual faculties rather than human relatives."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q15", "question": "What is the force of the command to persist compared with 18:28?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q15/p1", "position": "The excerpt raises the contrast but gives no answer.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī asks how keeping oneself steadfast in 18:28 differs from persisting in prayer with one's family here."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q16", "question": "What does 'We ask you no provision' deny?", "turns_on": "The object implicitly supplied for rizq: God's own provision or payment, the Prophet's and family's livelihood, other creatures' livelihood, or compensation for prophethood.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q16/p1", "position": "God asks no sustenance or payment from the Prophet for Himself; He asks worship, which benefits people.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Abū Muslim compare 51:56–57. Farrāʾ says no payment is asked; Ṭabarī contrasts bodily work with wealth. Jishumī compares worldly kings' extraction; Rāzī, Ṭabrisī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī stress divine independence. Ibn ʿĀshūr compares taxes and tribute and cites 51:56–58; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects the alternative that the object is provision for creatures or oneself."}, {"id": "20:132/q16/p2", "position": "He is not required to secure livelihood for himself or his family.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā prefers this by extending al-Ḥasan's gloss of 51:57; Ibn Qutayba, Rāzī, Qurṭubī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Bursevī, and al-Ālūsī link it to freedom for worship and the Hereafter. Al-Thawrī says God does not burden him with seeking provision. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects reading the request this way."}, {"id": "20:132/q16/p3", "position": "He is not charged with providing for God's other creatures.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, Ibn Muslim, Jishumī, Baghawī, Ṭabrisī, and Biqāʿī explicitly include others' sustenance; Māwardī extends God's provision to every creature. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects to taking the request as provision for creatures."}, {"id": "20:132/q16/p4", "position": "He owes no provision in return for the gift of prophethood.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā reports this explanation from some interpreters."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q17", "question": "What does the wording of the provision statement do here?", "turns_on": "The commentators locate the rhetorical point in reassurance, rejection of tribute, an answer to anxiety, or independence from wealthy opponents.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q17/p1", "position": "It reassures the family that prayer will not cost them their livelihood.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says they should not abandon prayer for earning; Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn ʿĀshūr, and Islahi tie the assurance to freedom for the Hereafter and the Prophet's task. Qushayrī says the promise consoles the poor when provision is delayed."}, {"id": "20:132/q17/p2", "position": "It reverses the tribute expected by earthly rulers and displays divine favor and independence.", "reasons": "Māwardī says God benefits every creature without receiving benefit. Jishumī contrasts worldly kings, Ibn ʿĀshūr taxes and tribute, and Asad a jealous deity; Rāzī says prayer benefits people alone. Study Quran compares the assurance with 51:57–58, where God asks no provision from people."}, {"id": "20:132/q17/p3", "position": "It answers anxiety about where provision will come from.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says the answer invokes God's boundless dominion and unexpected means; his next note says no provision concern rivals prayer."}, {"id": "20:132/q17/p4", "position": "It explains that preaching needs no patronage from wealthy opponents.", "reasons": "Islahi says the Prophet and his companions depend on God's support rather than the opponents' wealth."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q18", "question": "How is 'We ask you no provision' placed in the sentence?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q18/p1", "position": "It is parenthetical between the prayer command and God's assurance of provision.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies this sentence-level placement."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q19", "question": "Whom does 'We provide for you' include?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular pronoun only states the Prophet's direct address or also carries family, community, and universal provision.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q19/p1", "position": "The Prophet, with his family or all believers included in the promise.", "reasons": "Māwardī and Ṭabrisī extend divine provision to all creatures. Jishumī states provision to the Prophet. Biqāʿī includes the family; Islahi explains the singular pronoun by the Prophet's headship of the Muslim family, encompassing all Muslims, and compares a ruler's duty to provide for the community. He cites Abū Bakr and ʿUmar's concern for their people, including ʿUmar's fear of responsibility for a distant hungry dog. Ibn al-Jawzī-zād pairs the Prophet's and other creatures' freedom from the burden of providing with God's undertaking of provision."}, {"id": "20:132/q19/p2", "position": "The Prophet is specifically addressed as the recipient of the earlier promised provision.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr links the singular promise to 20:131, where the Lord's provision is better and lasting."}]}

e' understood?", "turns_on": "Whether fronting conveys exclusivity or emphasis.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q20/p1", "position": "It restricts the provision to God.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this as one force of fronting; Qushayrī says creatures have no causal power over provision."}, {"id": "20:132/q20/p2", "position": "It adds emphasis to the divine promise.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī gives this as the other possibility."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q21", "question": "How is narzuquka read?", "turns_on": "Whether the qāf is voiced with ḍamma, left still, or merged into kāf, and whether the word boundary permits assimilation.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q21/p1", "position": "The qāf has ḍamma and remains distinct.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān give this as the majority reading; al-Lawāmiʿ explains Abū ʿAmr's avoidance of qāf-to-kāf assimilation at a stopping point."}, {"id": "20:132/q21/p2", "position": "The qāf is still.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes this to a group."}, {"id": "20:132/q21/p3", "position": "The qāf is assimilated into the following kāf.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī name Ibn Waththāb, Yaʿqūb, and a group; al-Lawāmiʿ says assimilating readers treat the ending as medial or avoid stopping. Samīn notes Ibn Waththāb usually assimilates only with a following plural mīm, citing 2:21."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q22", "question": "Does the assurance of provision license leaving work?", "turns_on": "Whether divine provision replaces ordinary livelihood or only protects the priority of prayer.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q22/p1", "position": "No; lawful earning continues, and only work that obstructs required prayer must yield.", "reasons": "Rāzī cites 24:37, whose pious traders are not distracted from remembrance; al-Ālūsī says the general address permits leaving earning only when it prevents prayer and clarifies that persistence does not mean praying all day and night."}, {"id": "20:132/q22/p2", "position": "Some infer that the command must be Prophet-specific to avoid authorizing everyone to abandon earning.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports and rejects this inference; his reply limits the effect of the general command to conflicts with prayer."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q23", "question": "What effects of worship and prayer on provision are described?", "turns_on": "Whether provision is described as material relief, fixed allotment, witnessing the Provider, or spiritual knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q23/p1", "position": "Prayer and devotion open provision or relieve want, sometimes unexpectedly.", "reasons": "Qushayrī calls prayer a door to provision. Ibn Kathīr cites 65:2–3 and 51:56–58; a divine report via Abū Hurayra promises inner richness and relief from poverty for devotion, with the opposite for neglect. Biqāʿī records al-Tirmidhī's ḥasan gharīb grading of that report. Reports from Ibn Masʿūd and Zayd ibn Thābit contrast focus on the Hereafter, order and inner wealth with scattered worldly cares. Wahb says earlier believers often found relief through prayer. Islahi says only experience conveys prayer's guarantee and cites devout lives. Nasafī adds the maxim that whoever occupies himself with God's work receives God's care."}, {"id": "20:132/q23/p2", "position": "Provision is allotted by God, unaffected by greater or lesser pursuit.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says neither diligence nor neglect changes each person's eternally allotted share; trusting God yields contentment, while reliance on one's own effort yields toil."}, {"id": "20:132/q23/p3", "position": "The elect are nourished by witnessing the Provider, beyond material provision.", "reasons": "Qushayrī distinguishes provisions that strengthen souls from witnessing the Provider that strengthens hearts; ordinary people live by provisions, the elect by witnessing God. Realizing the divine 'We' erases distinctions between kinds of provision; prayer heals and nourishes the heart especially when bodily sustenance is delayed."}, {"id": "20:132/q23/p4", "position": "God's provision includes higher knowledge and freedom from dependence on people.", "reasons": "Qāshānī contrasts lower-world perfections and sensory knowledge with spiritual knowledge and holy realities. Bursevī says inward forms of prayer free their practitioners from dependence on people, cites 93:8, and quotes the Prophet's saying that his Lord feeds and gives him drink at night."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q24", "question": "What does al-ʿāqibah mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the word itself denotes only a good end or can denote any consequence, with the context fixing its value.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q24/p1", "position": "The praiseworthy final outcome.", "reasons": "Jishumī, Baghawī, Ṭabrisī, Abū Ḥayyān, and Bursevī give the favorable sense; Bursevī says an unqualified ʿāqibah denotes the good reward, Paradise. Qurṭubī says others have outcomes too, but a blameworthy one is rhetorically treated as nonexistent."}, {"id": "20:132/q24/p2", "position": "Whatever follows an affair, good or bad, though common usage favors good.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr gives the broad lexical sense, then says piety's result is good."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q25", "question": "What is the good outcome promised to piety?", "turns_on": "Whether the stated end is specifically Paradise, the wider favorable consequence of piety, an inward transformation, or an image of piety's sole value.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q25/p1", "position": "Paradise, the final reward of the God-fearing.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Yaḥyā, Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Suddī in Wāḥidī, Wāḥidī's Wajīz, Qurṭubī, Bursevī, Durr, and Study Quran identify Paradise. Yaḥyā cites 43:35; Qurṭubī says a blameworthy outcome counts as no true outcome. Al-Ālūsī reports al-Suddī's narrower identification while allowing a broader good end."}, {"id": "20:132/q25/p2", "position": "A praiseworthy end or ultimate success for the God-fearing, in this life or the next.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī speaks of the final outcome of deeds, not the heedless; Ibn ʿAṭiyya names victory here and mercy hereafter; Ibn Kathīr includes both worlds, ending in Paradise. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the Hereafter claim is absolute and worldly good possible. Islahi treats the verse as glad tidings of ultimate success after worldly sustenance; al-Ālūsī says the end is broader than Paradise. Ibn Kathīr cites an authentic dream report: dates from Ibn Ṭāb foretold believers' good worldly outcome, elevation, and sound religion."}, {"id": "20:132/q25/p3", "position": "The true end is inward detachment or disciplined self and limbs.", "reasons": "Sulamī reports Abū ʿUthmān: restraint from all that knowledge does not permit; Bursevī repeats this. Qāshānī reads the worthy end as shedding bodily garments and psychic dispositions. Al-Ālūsī makes the spiritual end two-sided: people of spiritual strength shed psychic vices and acquire spiritual virtues."}, {"id": "20:132/q25/p4", "position": "It is like a market where only piety has value.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports this image as another explanation of why the outcome belongs to piety."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q26", "question": "Who are the people of piety in the ending?", "turns_on": "Whether the expression is read through its people or emphasizes piety as the named possessor of the outcome.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q26/p1", "position": "Those who fear God and obey, including believers who affirm and follow the Prophet.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās in Wāḥidī, Baghawī, and Ṭabrisī specifies affirmation, following, and fear of God. Wāḥidī's Wajīz and Bursevī name the Prophet and believers. Ṭabarī contrasts them with those who neither fear punishment nor hope for reward; Asad glosses taqwā as God-consciousness."}, {"id": "20:132/q26/p2", "position": "The abstract piety stands for the pious person or people.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash gives 'people of piety'; Qushayrī notes naming a person by the verbal noun, and Samīn and al-Ālūsī compare 7:128. Nasafī says two annexed nouns are elided; al-Ālūsī adds that omission highlights piety itself."}, {"id": "20:132/q26/p3", "position": "People of spiritual strength who shed psychic vices and acquire spiritual virtues.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī identifies the recipients of the worthy final outcome by this inward transformation."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q27", "question": "How does the grammar of li-l-taqwā assign the outcome?", "turns_on": "Whether the construction is explained through an omitted possessor or the lām's assertion of possession.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q27/p1", "position": "An understood 'people of' makes the outcome belong to the pious.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash, Qushayrī, Samīn, Nasafī, and al-Ālūsī explain the abstract noun for its bearers; Nasafī posits two omitted annexed nouns, while al-Ālūsī says omitting the noun foregrounds piety. Samīn and al-Ālūsī cite 7:128."}, {"id": "20:132/q27/p2", "position": "The lām marks possession of the good outcome.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says it confirms the intended favorable consequence; the claim is absolute for the Hereafter and possible for worldly good."}]}

Biqāʿī says zakāt is omitted because the previous verse already discourages attachment. Ibn ʿĀshūr sees ahl answering the preceding mention of spouses, so family finds enjoyment in prayer; Islahi says no patronage from opponents is needed."}, {"id": "20:132/q28/p2", "position": "The prior praise command and this prayer command mark the Prophet's elevated rank.", "reasons":

{"id": "20:132/q29", "question": "How does the ending connect to the prayer command and other verses?", "turns_on": "Which Qurʾānic context is used to explain the final statement.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q29/p1", "position": "It completes the prayer counsel by stating that piety yields the good end.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the sentence is coordinated with God's not asking provision and explains persistence in prayer; it forms a universal proverb. Study Quran points to 7:128, 11:49, and 28:83; Yaḥyā cites 43:35."}, {"id": "20:132/q29/p2", "position": "It echoes 22:37: what reaches God is piety, not sacrificial meat or blood.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī makes this connection while stressing God's independence from provision."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q30", "question": "How does this passage continue the earlier call to patience?", "turns_on": "The connection can be the continuing patience theme or the earlier command's prayer practice.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q30/p1", "position": "The following objection of the opponents continues the call to endure their speech.", "reasons": "Rāzī links the next account to 20:130, after the counsel on patience and prayer."}, {"id": "20:132/q30/p2", "position": "The family command extends the earlier daily prayer and glorification instruction.", "reasons": "Islahi identifies the prayer of 20:130 with the vigilant prayer here. {"id": "20:132/q31", "question": "What event is reported around the revelation of these verses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q31/p1", "position": "A Jewish lender demanded collateral when the Prophet sought a loan; the Prophet offered armor and these verses were revealed.", "reasons": "Abū Rāfiʿ's report in Ṭabarī includes a guest and links 15:87 with 20:131–132; Wāḥidī's Wajīz says the lender's demand saddened the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q32", "question": "What is said about the revelation time of this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q32/p1", "position": "It is Meccan like the rest of the sūra, probably early Meccan.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī finds no authority excluding it as Medinan; he infers an early date from daily prayers, patience, and the warning against unbelievers' wealth. Ibn Masʿūd calls Sūrat Ṭā Hā one of the earliest old sūras. He notes the tension between this timing and the apparent Medinan setting of door-visit reports."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q33", "question": "What lexical information is supplied about ahl beyond the referent?", "turns_on": "Whether the lexical note gives the ordinary and extended sense of ahl or only associated root vocabulary.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q33/p1", "position": "Ahl ordinarily denotes blood relatives, with broader figurative uses shown by context.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī defines the ordinary kinship bond and says context permits extension; Islahi argues for the wider Arabic use and cites Abū Bakr's expression and 19:55."}, {"id": "20:132/q33/p2", "position": "The lexical excursus also notes ihāla for melted fat and istaʾhala for eating it.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī records these cognate words without making them the verse's referent."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q34", "question": "What prayer-related remedy is drawn from Jonah's case or an epidemic?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q34/p1", "position": "Prayer or glorification is invoked as a remedy in distress.", "reasons": "Bursevī quotes Ibn ʿAbbās on Jonah's prayer and 37:143: without it he would have remained in the fish. He reports al-Shāfiʿī's inference that glorification is especially beneficial against an epidemic."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q35", "question": "What is the rhetorical point of the comparison with night in the ancillary notes?", "turns_on": "Whether the comparison takes only universal reach or also a connotation of pursuit.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q35/p1", "position": "Night illustrates universal reach without importing its darkness into the comparison.", "reasons": "The Prophet's report says Islam will reach wherever night reaches; Jurjānī explains that an incidental unfavorable feature need not be counted. He compares the sun as apt for a welcome blessing and says even seemingly harsh praise can be hyperbolic rather than insulting."}, {"id": "20:132/q35/p2", "position": "The choice of night may also suggest someone evading a resentful pursuer.", "reasons": "Jurjānī says day and night both reach everywhere, but offers this possible defense of night as the chosen image."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q36", "question": "What general treatments of hamza are described in the ancillary notes?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish phonetic practice and exceptions from disputed reports about early pronunciation.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q36/p1", "position": "Hamza may be softened by transfer of its vowel or substitution as a long vowel, with stated exceptions.", "reasons": "Itqān says hamza is hard to articulate and Quraysh and the Hijaz commonly softened it, often in Ibn Kathīr, Warsh from Nāfiʿ, and Abū ʿAmr. Warsh's naql transfers the vowel to a preceding still final consonant, as in qad aflaḥa; Yaʿqūb's transmitters from Warsh retain hamza in kitābiyah innī ẓanantu. Abū ʿAmr's ibdāl changes still hamza to a long vowel. The chapter selects four broad kinds but the excerpt details two."}, {"id": "20:132/q36/p2", "position": "Hamza is retained where stillness, difficulty, or ambiguity requires it.", "reasons": "Itqān says jussive and construct-state stillness, or a harder and ambiguous result from dropping hamza, preserve it; moving hamza is always verified."}, {"id": "20:132/q36/p3", "position": "Reports claim the Prophet and early caliphs omitted hamza, or distinguish nabī from nabīʾ.", "reasons": "The Ibn ʿUmar report via Nāfiʿ claims nonpronunciation until later; Abū Shāma rejects it because Mūsā ibn ʿUbayda is weak. An Abū Dharr report says the Prophet corrected nabīʾ; al-Dhahabī calls it anomalous and Ḥumrān untrustworthy."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q37", "question": "What reading is reported for innaka lā in the ancillary note?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q37/p1", "position": "Nāfiʿ and Abū Bakr read the hamza with kasra; the others use fatḥa.", "reasons": "Nashr gives the two reader groups for this cited phrase."}]}
{"id": "21:1/q01", "question": "What does iqtaraba mean and add to qaruba?", "turns_on": "Whether the augmented form conveys emphasis beyond the shared root meaning.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q01/p1", "position": "It means to draw near; the augmented form can emphasize nearness.", "reasons": "Al-Mubarrad, al-Baḥr, al-Biqāʿī, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī find emphasis in its expanded form; al-Biqāʿī connects it to this being the final community. Jishumī says qurb is opposite distance, literal spatially but also temporal or circumstantial."}, {"id": "21:1/q01/p2", "position": "It has the same basic sense as qaruba, without requiring additional force.", "reasons": "Jishumī treats qurb and iqtirāb as equivalent; Abū Ḥayyān and others also give the basic equivalence while reporting possible emphasis."}]}
{"id": "21:1/q02", "question": "What is drawing near in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether ḥisāb directly names final accounting, its time, a worldly requital, or death.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q02/p1", "position": "The resurrection and God's actual accounting of deeds draw near.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī explicitly rejects supplying 'time' as an omitted noun: the account itself approaches. Al-Rāzī says spatial approach is impossible."}, {"id": "21:1/q02/p2", "position": "The time of the Hour or of people's reckoning draws near.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj supplies 'time'; al-Rāzī says the proximity must be temporal; 54:1 and 21:97 provide parallels. Al-Ālūsī says saying 'account' evokes the Hour's fearful effects; Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that the context would then say Day or time."}, {"id": "21:1/q02/p3", "position": "A near worldly punishment, especially Mecca's defeat at Badr, is meant.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says Meccans mocked delayed punishment and were killed at Badr. Al-Biqāʿī includes Badr and the Conquest; al-Būrsawī prefers Badr because death immediately connects to resurrection. Iṣlāḥī connects near accountability to a messenger's conclusive warning and a nation's destruction."}, {"id": "21:1/q02/p4", "position": "It concerns each person's near death or minor resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says understanding resurrection would allow witnessing one's account now. Al-Qurṭubī says each person's death is their Hour; Study Quran reports death as sufficient reason to call reckoning near."}, {"id": "21:1/q02/p5", "position": "It concerns what people have been promised, including worldly affairs.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj calls it what was promised; the report of Abū Hurayra in al-Durr connects the approaching account with worldly affairs."}]}

{"id": "21:1/q04", "question": "Why use a past-tense form for the approaching account?", "turns_on": "Whether the tense marks certainty or a temporally occurring approach.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q04/p1", "position": "It expresses certainty that the Day of Judgment will come.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu gives the certainty of its occurrence as the reason for the past tense."}, {"id": "21:1/q04/p2", "position": "It presents approach as already begun, with real temporal progress.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports that an unchanging nearness from creation would call for an ongoing form; a critic answers that most of the world's span had elapsed by the Prophet's mission. {"id": "21:1/q05", "question": "How does the lām in lil-nās work?", "turns_on": "Whether the preposition attaches to 'approached', stands for min or ilā, or reinforces the possessive construction.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q05/p1", "position": "It is governed by iqtaraba as its complement.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Bayḍāwī give this as the straightforward analysis; al-Nasafī calls it an added connective. Abū Ḥayyān objects to possessive emphasis as unattested, ungoverned, and out of order; al-Ālūsī prefers verbal attachment."}, {"id": "21:1/q05/p2", "position": "It stands for min, expressing approach from or relative to the people.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Māwardī's successors and al-ʿUyūn give min. Al-Ālūsī says min can mark an endpoint, cites al-Shumnī and Ibn Mālik's 'approached from him' for 'approached him', and rejects deriving it from a starting point; al-Raḍī explains preposition use by analogy with an opposite verb."}, {"id": "21:1/q05/p3", "position": "It means toward the people, like ilā.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says min would measure from the object and ilā toward it; the verse depicts accounting coming at the people. Al-Ālūsī accepts ilā as the more characteristic endpoint marker but rejects restricting the phrase to it."}, {"id": "21:1/q05/p4", "position": "It reinforces the possessive relation in 'their account'.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī compares Arabic expressions such as 'their departure drew near for the people'; al-Bayḍāwī says it develops 'people's account' to 'their account'. Al-Samīn defends analogy with lā abā laka; Abū Ḥayyān and the Shaykh object that examples differ, the governor is missing, and the lām is wrongly ordered. Al-Ālūsī finds it strained."}, {"id": "21:1/q05/p5", "position": "It cannot be parsed by replacing lil-nās with a later group or by displacing a hidden element.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās rejects placing an implicit element before the explicit element that it is meant to follow. Al-Zarkashī rejects strained substitution of 'those who wronged' for 'the people' and compares another legally driven parsing."}]}
{"id": "21:1/q06", "question": "Why put 'for the people' before 'their account'?", "turns_on": "Whether fronting primarily hastens alarm, evokes pursuit, or strengthens the possessive relation.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q06/p1", "position": "It delivers the threat immediately and makes the delayed subject frightening.", "reasons": "Al-ʿUyūn says fronting hastens dread; al-Biqāʿī and others say delaying 'their account' leaves listeners imagining what terrible thing approaches. Al-Ālūsī says this can be the intended effect even if heedless hearers do not fear."}, {"id": "21:1/q06/p2", "position": "It pictures the people as pursued by an approaching danger.", "reasons": "A rhetorician cited by al-Ālūsī says the verb and fronted phrase depict an advancing thing chasing a fleeing target, conveying danger. Abū al-Suʿūd adds that attributing approach to the account magnifies it as a pursuer that inevitably catches people; al-Ālūsī approves."}, {"id": "21:1/q06/p3", "position": "It reinforces the account's attribution and restriction to those people.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī says the fronted expression, lām and definite article together strengthen the possessive sense and restriction; al-Ālūsī reports objections to the underlying parsing."}]}
{"id": "21:1/q07", "question": "Who are 'the people'?", "turns_on": "Whether the general noun keeps its full range or is restricted by the following descriptions and historical threat.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q07/p1", "position": "They are the Meccan polytheists or deniers of resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī, Ibn ʿAbbās and others cite the ensuing heedlessness, playful hearing and accusation of magic in 21:2–3. {"id": "21:1/q08", "question": "What is the sense of nās here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q08/p1", "position": "Nās is linked to naws, a restless instability in human beings.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says restlessness prevents settled security and steadiness, a deficiency from which few are saved."}]}
{"id": "21:1/q09", "question": "What does ḥisāb mean?", "turns_on": "Whether ḥisāb names the accounting process, the resulting punishment, a counted quantity, or a promised event.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q09/p1", "position": "It is God's accounting of people's deeds and blessings, with recompense for good or evil.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī specifies inquiry into deeds, blessings and obedience; al-Būrsawī says it discloses what is for and against someone so recompense follows. {"id": "21:1/q11", "question": "What does 'their' in 'their account' emphasize?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronoun is read as general human responsibility or a targeted Meccan threat.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q11/p1", "position": "The addressees themselves must answer for deeds and divine blessings.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says they will answer for blessings and obedience; Ibn al-Zubayr connects 20:131 and 102:8 with the previous warning against coveting worldly goods; Kur'an Yolu frames life, death, and blessings as a test calling for gratitude and obedience."}, {"id": "21:1/q11/p2", "position": "The account of sinful Meccan polytheists is at issue.", "reasons": "Al-Būrsawī links their evil deeds to resurrection and al-Biqāʿī to possible Badr reprisal."}]}
{"id": "21:1/q12", "question": "What is ghafla?", "turns_on": "Whether ghafla means bare inattention, ignorance of the outcome, or deliberate neglect.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q12/p1", "position": "It is inattention or lack of vigilance and alertness.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī calls it loss of a meaning from the mind, opposite to alertness; al-Būrsawī traces it to insufficient vigilance."}, {"id": "21:1/q12/p2", "position": "It is ignorance of the reckoning and what God will do.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī glosses it as ignorance; exegetes say people do not know what awaits them. {"id": "21:1/q13", "question": "What kind of heedlessness is condemned here?", "turns_on": "Whether the description is denial, worldly absorption, sinful failure to prepare, or inward absorption in God.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q13/p1", "position": "They fail to contemplate or prepare for the final account.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says worldly life keeps them from reflecting on its severe trials. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī add that reason points to requital of good and evil. Al-Būrsawī stresses outright denial, beyond simple carelessness; al-Ālūsī warns that heedlessness about requital produces every error. Al-Biqāʿī says resurrection or deadly events expose their heedlessness and humble survivors, who then discern truth from falsehood."}, {"id": "21:1/q13/p2", "position": "They are engrossed in worldly life and desire, ignoring the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Reports attributed to the Prophet identify worldly life; al-Qushayrī says this alienation ends only at death. {"id": "21:1/q14", "question": "Who is described as heedless and turning away?", "turns_on": "Whether the ensuing traits restrict the general noun to polytheists or can also characterize believers.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q14/p1", "position": "The description singles out unbelievers, especially Meccan polytheists.", "reasons": "The following verses describe disbelievers' play and accusations; Ibn al-Jawzī says the account's approach is universal while this description is specific. {"id": "21:1/q15", "question": "What are they turning away from?", "turns_on": "Which warning or object their aversion concerns.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q15/p1", "position": "They turn from preparing for and thinking about their reckoning.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī and other commentators pair heedlessness with lack of preparation; al-Zamakhsharī says they shut their ears to warnings once roused."}, {"id": "21:1/q15/p2", "position": "They turn from faith, the Qur'an, the Prophet's message, signs and warnings.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā says they turn from the Qur'an; ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās says from what Muḥammad brought. {"id": "21:1/q16", "question": "What does muʿriḍūn imply lexically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q16/p1", "position": "Aʿraḍa is to turn aside while exposing one's side.", "reasons": "Al-Būrsawī gives the physical source of the figurative aversion."}]}
{"id": "21:1/q17", "question": "How can they be both heedless and turning away?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrases describe successive responses, a state beside an action, or a broader sense of neglect.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q17/p1", "position": "They initially fail to think of the outcome, then deliberately ignore warnings that awaken them.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī explain the sequence; al-Kashf distinguishes persistent neglect of rational proofs from rejection when scriptural proofs are presented. {"id": "21:1/q18", "question": "How is the closing clause parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the inner prepositional phrase is a predicate or a circumstance, and how the whole clause attaches.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q18/p1", "position": "The wāw introduces a circumstantial clause describing the people.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī and al-Jishumī identify the wāw; Sībawayh equates it to idh and cites 8:11. {"id": "21:1/q19", "question": "What does the verse teach about rational and revealed proof of requital?", "turns_on": "Whether reason independently establishes the moral premise of reward and punishment.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q19/p1", "position": "Requital for good and evil is required by reason and divine wisdom.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī say reason requires it; al-Būrsawī argues treating obedience and sin alike would violate wisdom and justice. {"id": "21:1/q21", "question": "What spiritual response should the near account prompt?", "turns_on": "Which conduct follows from taking the warning seriously.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q21/p1", "position": "People should repent, prepare, reckon themselves, and shorten worldly hopes.", "reasons": "Sulamī's authorities urge waking, vigilance and self-accounting; al-Rāzī says nearness and concealed timing promote repentance. {"id": "21:1/q22", "question": "Why leave the exact time of the account unstated?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q22/p1", "position": "Concealing it encourages preparation, like concealing the time of death.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says the unspecified time benefits those obligated to repent; al-Būrsawī likewise calls concealment more fitting."}]}
